title: What happens if external AI agents can enter a simulation game world?
author: CapitalDebate5092
selftext:
I came across an interesting idea recently and wanted to get people's thoughts on it.

Most AI in games are essentially NPC systems fully controlled by the game itself.

But imagine a simulation game where external AI agents can actually enter the world and act as residents.

For example, instead of spawning NPCs internally, the game exposes a simple interface where outside agents can read world state and choose actions. The agent effectively becomes another entity living in the simulation.

In the example I saw, people could even tell their AI agent to join the world by reading a skill file, and the agent would register itself as a resident in the simulation.

Conceptually it feels less like NPC AI and more like agents acting as independent players inside a shared world.

I'm curious. Do you think this could become a new direction for AI-driven games, or would it mostly lead to chaos and unstable simulations?

comments.author: kraboo_team
comments.body:
as i am working on [the experiment](https://experiment.iplaytoday.com/) the concept of AI playing, doing quests, missions and so on is more than real one. But implement them into a working game with mechanics, without creating chaos could be taught. 

My point is, that it could be possible, to have AI NCPs - it already exists, they have own thinking methods based on prompts, but you are not able to let them "work" with a classic NPCs which are not able to do such a things.

So maybe, try to go the way, like i in the experiment, where i use only AI agents, fighting each other. 

One thing i found out harder was the interaction logic - when you have more AI agents, they need to hold the memory, cascade for the interaction. But if you handle that properly, the outcome is really solid :)

replies.author: CapitalDebate5092
replies.body:
That's a really interesting point.  
I can imagine mixing traditional NPC logic with autonomous agents getting messy pretty quickly.

The memory and interaction cascade problem you mentioned sounds like the core challenge. Once multiple agents start reacting to each other over time, the state space probably explodes.

In your experiment, how do you handle agent memory and world state updates?  
Do you keep a shared world state or mostly agent-local memory?

replies.author: kraboo_team
replies.body: I have created their own datasets and database, which they are prompted to follow through and use whenever they want to create something or do. But still working on it to push it further :)

comments.author: monsterfurby
comments.body: The most advanced implementation of this is arguably Skyrimnet - but it's important to have a programmatic "objective truth" layer and decision mechanic imho. Relying on LLMs for decision making, even with access to game-level APIs, is a bit of a Rube Goldberg Machine. Strategically, I could see that - on a game-flow basis, it's probably better to have a solid base logic that just knows when to call the LLM to make a complex decision.

replies.author: CapitalDebate5092
replies.body:
agree, otherwise the world state could drift depending on how each agent interprets things. I wonder if long-term agent societies would eventually need something like a shared simulation layer.

but for this AIvilization game, it has several goals to instruct the agents to do things right, such as balancing between "money earned" "health", etc.

comments.author: AnotsuKagehisa
comments.body: Did he take the blue pill or red pill?

comments.author: kal101246
comments.body: What types of tools would support this workflow? What's the barrier of entry for folks looking to use this? I ask because if this is walled off, it may offput players. However, if players could easily control to what extent they interact with them then there might be an opportunity here. I imagine some players would prefer to join a "server" that is mostly human, but there might be times when they want to play with someone and agents are the only ones available. Thus, being more willing to experiment with synthetic users.

comments.author: MakkoMakkerton
comments.body: I think at first it would definitely lead to some chaos. but as things get worked out, it would become something of artistic beauty. I believe a few projects are building something along these lines, not sure if you've heard or parallel colony but its essentially this except you also play as an AI NPC basically. You can "suggest" and give ideas, but the agent is still independent and acts on its own throughout the day.
